claim: Cutaneous metastatic melanoma is the deadliest form of skin cancer, and its occurrence is growing.
source: Cutaneous metastatic melanoma is the deadliest form of skin cancer, and its occurrence is growing (Moran et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moran et al., 2018

claim: Median overall survival of patients with advanced-stage melanoma has increased from ~9 months to at least 2 years since 2011.
source: Indeed, median overall survival (OS) of patients with advanced-stage melanoma has increased from ~9 months to at least 2 years since 2011 (Luke et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Luke et al., 2017

claim: OS is better after targeted therapies.
source: OS is better after targeted (Teterycz et al., 2019) or immunotherapies (Weiss et al., 2019), but there are still non-responders and neo/acquired resistants.

claim: OS is better after immunotherapies.

claim: There are still non-responders and neo/acquired resistants to targeted and immunotherapies.

claim: Melanoma has a CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP).

evidence: Supported by citation to Tanemura et al., 2009

claim: Several methylated genes are associated with melanoma progression.
source: Melanoma has a CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP) (Tanemura et al., 2009), and several methylated genes are associated with melanoma progression (Micevic et al., 2017), with aggressive clinical and pathological features and poor survival in patients (de Unamuno Bustos et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2019), are candidate epigenetic drivers of melanoma metastasis (Chatterjee et al., 2017), or are implicated in immunotherapy resistance (Emran et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Micevic et al., 2017

claim: Several methylated genes are associated with aggressive clinical and pathological features and poor survival in patients.

source: Melanoma has a CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP) (Tanemura et al., 2009), and several methylated genes are associated with melanoma progression (Micevic et al., 2017), with aggressive clinical and pathological features and poor survival in patients (de Unamuno Bustos et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2019), are candidate epigenetic drivers of melanoma metastasis (Chatterjee et al., 2017), or are implicated in immunotherapy resistance (Emran et al., 2019).

claim: DNA methylation has been shown to occur very early in tumour formation.
source: Importantly, DNA methylation has been shown to occur very early in tumour formation (Michalak et al., 2019) and thus has the potential to provide early biomarkers indicating the metastatic potential of the tumour.

claim: DNA methylation has the potential to provide early biomarkers indicating the metastatic potential of the tumour.
source: Importantly, DNA methylation has been shown to occur very early in tumour formation (Michalak et al., 2019) and thus has the potential to provide early biomarkers indicating the metastatic potential of the tumour.

claim: The WM115 cell line was derived from a human primary melanoma in early stages of the vertical growth phase.
source: The first pair consisted of the WM115 and WM266-4 cell lines, derived from a vertical growth phase (VGP) primary melanoma and a cutaneous metastasis from the same patient, respectively, thus comparing a less and more aggressive pair of human melanoma cells.
evidence: Stated as a description of the cell line model used in the study

claim: The WM266-4 cell line was derived from a cutaneous metastasis from the same patient as WM115.
source: The first pair consisted of the WM115 and WM266-4 cell lines, derived from a vertical growth phase (VGP) primary melanoma and a cutaneous metastasis from the same patient, respectively, thus comparing a less and more aggressive pair of human melanoma cells.
evidence: Stated as a description of the cell line model used in the study

claim: The M4Be cell line was established from a human lymph node metastasis.
source: The second and the third pairs include a cell line established from a human lymph node metastasis (M4Be) and two metastatic variants selected for their increased metastatic potential in xenograft experiments either in mouse (M4BeS2) or in rat (TW12) (Figure 1A, step 1).
evidence: Stated as a description of the cell line model used in the study

claim: M4BeS2 is a metastatic variant of M4Be selected for increased metastatic potential in mouse xenograft experiments.
source: The second and the third pairs include a cell line established from a human lymph node metastasis (M4Be) and two metastatic variants selected for their increased metastatic potential in xenograft experiments either in mouse (M4BeS2) or in rat (TW12) (Figure 1A, step 1).
evidence: Stated as a description of the cell line model used in the study

claim: TW12 is a metastatic variant of M4Be selected for increased metastatic potential in rat xenograft experiments.
source: The second and the third pairs include a cell line established from a human lymph node metastasis (M4Be) and two metastatic variants selected for their increased metastatic potential in xenograft experiments either in mouse (M4BeS2) or in rat (TW12) (Figure 1A, step 1).
evidence: Stated as a description of the cell line model used in the study

claim: 2783 genes were hypermethylated in WM266-4 vs WM115.
source: After applying this differential threshold to at least three CpG positions for each gene, we found that 2783, 1645, and 1641 genes were hypermethylated in WM266-4 vs WM115, M4BeS2 vs M4Be, and TW12 vs M4Be, respectively (A).
evidence: Reported as a result from the 450K array analysis

claim: 1645 genes were hypermethylated in M4BeS2 vs M4Be.
source: After applying this differential threshold to at least three CpG positions for each gene, we found that 2783, 1645, and 1641 genes were hypermethylated in WM266-4 vs WM115, M4BeS2 vs M4Be, and TW12 vs M4Be, respectively (A).
evidence: Reported as a result from the 450K array analysis

claim: 1641 genes were hypermethylated in TW12 vs M4Be.
source: After applying this differential threshold to at least three CpG positions for each gene, we found that 2783, 1645, and 1641 genes were hypermethylated in WM266-4 vs WM115, M4BeS2 vs M4Be, and TW12 vs M4Be, respectively (A).
evidence: Reported as a result from the 450K array analysis

claim: 229 genes were commonly hypermethylated in all three pairs of cell lines.
source: 229 genes, comprising 5590 CpG sites, were common to all three pairs of cell lines.
evidence: Reported as a result from the comparative analysis of the three cell line pairs

claim: The 229 common hypermethylated genes comprise 5590 CpG sites.
source: 229 genes, comprising 5590 CpG sites, were common to all three pairs of cell lines.
evidence: Reported as a result from the comparative analysis

claim: 1287 (23%) CpGs were hypermethylated (>20%) in WM266-4 cells.
source: 1287 (23%) CpGs were hypermethylated (>20%) in WM266-4 cells of which 788 (61%) were located in promoter regions (TSS1500-TSS200-5'UTR-first exon), 452 (35%) in gene bodies and 47 (4%) in 3'UTR regions.
evidence: Reported as a result from the analysis of the 229 genes in WM115/WM266-4 pair

claim: 788 (61%) of the hypermethylated CpGs in WM266-4 cells were located in promoter regions.
source: 1287 (23%) CpGs were hypermethylated (>20%) in WM266-4 cells of which 788 (61%) were located in promoter regions (TSS1500-TSS200-5'UTR-first exon), 452 (35%) in gene bodies and 47 (4%) in 3'UTR regions.
evidence: Reported as a result from the genomic location analysis

claim: 452 (35%) of the hypermethylated CpGs in WM266-4 cells were located in gene bodies.
source: 1287 (23%) CpGs were hypermethylated (>20%) in WM266-4 cells of which 788 (61%) were located in promoter regions (TSS1500-TSS200-5'UTR-first exon), 452 (35%) in gene bodies and 47 (4%) in 3'UTR regions.
evidence: Reported as a result from the genomic location analysis

claim: 47 (4%) of the hypermethylated CpGs in WM266-4 cells were located in 3'UTR regions.
source: 1287 (23%) CpGs were hypermethylated (>20%) in WM266-4 cells of which 788 (61%) were located in promoter regions (TSS1500-TSS200-5'UTR-first exon), 452 (35%) in gene bodies and 47 (4%) in 3'UTR regions.
evidence: Reported as a result from the genomic location analysis

claim: 116 of the 229 hypermethylated genes were associated with IPA canonical functions.
source: Using QIAGEN Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA, QIAGEN Redwood City, https://digitalinsights.qiagen.com/) software, we found 116 genes highly associated with known functions (p<0.05, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Reported as a result from IPA analysis

claim: Bootstrap analysis confirmed a non-random distribution of the 229 hypermethylated genes along the chromosomes.
source: Bootstrap analysis of the repartition of the 229 genes along the chromosomes confirmed a non-random distribution, and hypermethylated genes enriched in short chromosomal regions (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Reported as a result from statistical bootstrap analysis

claim: Hypermethylated genes are enriched in short chromosomal regions.
source: Bootstrap analysis of the repartition of the 229 genes along the chromosomes confirmed a non-random distribution, and hypermethylated genes enriched in short chromosomal regions (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Reported as a result from statistical bootstrap analysis

claim: Nine methylation clusters were identified on chromosomes 5, 6, 10, 15, 16, and 17.
source: Nine methylation clusters were identified on chromosomes 5, 6, 10, 15, 16, and 17 (dotted line circles in Figure 2 and list in Figure 2—figure supplement 2), containing a total of 74 genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Reported as a result from cluster analysis and shown in Figure 2

claim: The nine methylation clusters contain a total of 74 genes.
source: Nine methylation clusters were identified on chromosomes 5, 6, 10, 15, 16, and 17 (dotted line circles in Figure 2 and list in Figure 2—figure supplement 2), containing a total of 74 genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Reported as a result from cluster analysis

claim: 34 genes were selected because they displayed at least two hypermethylated CpGs located in the promoter region and a 40% difference in methylation when comparing human WM266-4 to WM115 cells.
source: Among these genes, 34 were further selected because they displayed at least two hypermethylated CpGs located in the promoter region (TSS1500-TSS200-5'UTR-first exon) and a 40% difference in methylation when comparing human WM266-4 to WM115 cells.
evidence: Reported as a selection criterion applied to the genes in clusters

claim: Chromosome 5 contains a methylation cluster with six genes belonging to the protocadherin beta (PCDHB) family.
source: On chromosome 5, nine genes were identified as hypermethylated with a methylation cluster containing six genes belonging to the protocadherin beta (PCDHB) family (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and insert).
evidence: Reported as a result from cluster analysis and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Chromosome 17 contains a methylation cluster that includes five members of the multigenic myosin heavy chain (MYH) family.
source: Interestingly, this methylation cluster included five members of the multigenic myosin heavy chain (MYH) family (insert in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Reported as a result from cluster analysis and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: SPAG7, SOCS3, and RAC3 displayed the strongest hypermethylation values (over 90%) among the 10 hypermethylated genes found on chromosome 17.
source: SPAG7, SOCS3, and RAC3 displayed the strongest hypermethylation values (over 90%) among the 10 hypermethylated genes found on chromosome 17 that had at least two CpGs in the promoter region with a >40% difference methylation in WM266-4 cells.
evidence: Reported as a result from methylation analysis of chromosome 17 genes

claim: 19 genes were common to both the oriented strategy (34 genes) and the non-oriented strategy (116 genes).
source: Finally, when cross-checking the 34 genes from the oriented strategy and the 116 genes from the non-oriented strategy, we identified 19 common genes (Figure 1B).
evidence: Reported as a result from cross-checking the two analytical strategies

claim: All 19 common genes were associated with one or two of the top functional networks from the IPA.
source: Notably, all of 19 genes were associated with one or two of the top functional networks from the IPA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Reported as a result from IPA functional analysis

claim: MYH1 is known to show aberrant expression levels in aggressive cells in head and neck squamous and lung carcinoma tumours.
source: MYH1 was selected because it forms a highly differentially methylated cluster (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and is known to show aberrant expression levels in aggressive cells in head and neck squamous and lung carcinoma tumours (Vachani et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vachani et al., 2007

claim: SOCS3 displayed among the highest hypermethylation peaks in aggressive melanoma lines (92%).
source: SOCS3 and RAC3 displayed among the highest hypermethylation peaks in our aggressive melanoma lines (92 and 96%, respectively), with a very high differential methylation score, above 70%, between WM266-4 and WM115 cells.
evidence: Reported as a result from methylation analysis

claim: RAC3 displayed among the highest hypermethylation peaks in aggressive melanoma lines (96%).
source: SOCS3 and RAC3 displayed among the highest hypermethylation peaks in our aggressive melanoma lines (92 and 96%, respectively), with a very high differential methylation score, above 70%, between WM266-4 and WM115 cells.
evidence: Reported as a result from methylation analysis

claim: SOCS3 has previously been reported to be hypermethylated in melanoma.
source: In addition, SOCS3 has previously been reported to be hypermethylated in melanoma (Tokita et al., 2007), while loss of RAC3 expression has been associated with impaired invasion in glioma and breast carcinoma cells (Chan et al., 2005; Baugher et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tokita et al., 2007

claim: Loss of RAC3 expression has been associated with impaired invasion in glioma and breast carcinoma cells.
source: In addition, SOCS3 has previously been reported to be hypermethylated in melanoma (Tokita et al., 2007), while loss of RAC3 expression has been associated with impaired invasion in glioma and breast carcinoma cells (Chan et al., 2005; Baugher et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chan et al., 2005 and Baugher et al., 2005

claim: HOXB2 has previously been associated with progression of bladder cancer when silenced by promoter hypermethylation.
source: It has previously been associated with progression of bladder cancer when silenced by promoter hypermethylation, and it can be re-expressed upon demethylation treatment with 5-azacitidine (5AzadC) (Marsit et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marsit et al., 2010

claim: HOXB2 can be re-expressed upon demethylation treatment with 5-azacitidine (5AzadC).
source: It has previously been associated with progression of bladder cancer when silenced by promoter hypermethylation, and it can be re-expressed upon demethylation treatment with 5-azacitidine (5AzadC) (Marsit et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marsit et al., 2010

claim: PCDHB15 and PCDHB16 are CIMP-associated with bad prognosis in neuroblastoma.
source: On chromosome 5, two genes were chosen from the PCDHB hypermethylation cluster: PCDHB15 and PCDHB16 that are CIMP-associated with bad prognosis in neuroblastoma (Abe et al., 2005; Banelli et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Abe et al., 2005 and Banelli et al., 2012

claim: Neurons and melanocytes originate from the same germ layer during embryogenesis.
source: Of note, neurons and melanocytes originate from the same germ layer during embryogenesis.
evidence: Stated as established biological knowledge

claim: BCL2L10 was previously described as hypermethylated in gastric cancer cell lines.
source: Furthermore, BCL2L10 (B cell lymphoma 2 like 10) located on chromosome 15 was selected because it bears the highest methylation score (73%) on this chromosome, it is implicated in apoptosis, it was previously described as hypermethylated in gastric cancer cell lines (Mikata et al., 2010), and associated with poor prognosis in gastric cancer patients (Xu et al., 2011; Voso et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mikata et al., 2010

claim: BCL2L10 is associated with poor prognosis in gastric cancer patients.
source: Furthermore, BCL2L10 (B cell lymphoma 2 like 10) located on chromosome 15 was selected because it bears the highest methylation score (73%) on this chromosome, it is implicated in apoptosis, it was previously described as hypermethylated in gastric cancer cell lines (Mikata et al., 2010), and associated with poor prognosis in gastric cancer patients (Xu et al., 2011; Voso et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Xu et al., 2011 and Voso et al., 2011

claim: MIR155HG encodes a microRNA, miR-155, that is linked to cell proliferation and cancer.
source: Finally, MIR155HG, located on chromosome 21, encodes a microRNA, miR-155, was chosen because linked to cell proliferation and cancer (Elton et al., 2013), including in melanoma where it is downregulated (Levati et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Elton et al., 2013

claim: miR-155 is downregulated in melanoma.
source: Finally, MIR155HG, located on chromosome 21, encodes a microRNA, miR-155, was chosen because linked to cell proliferation and cancer (Elton et al., 2013), including in melanoma where it is downregulated (Levati et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Levati et al., 2009 and Wang et al., 2020

claim: Seven genes passed the threshold of validation (20% DNA methylation difference between the cell lines) by DNA pyrosequencing.
source: The methylation status of these eight genes (MYH1, RAC3, SOCS3, HOXB2, PCDHB15, PCDHB16, BCL2L10, and MIR155HG) was further validated in WM115 vs WM266-4 cell lines by DNA pyrosequencing after bisulfite conversion and PCR amplification on 100 bp regions containing the CpGs identified in step 2 (Figure 1C). Seven genes pass the threshold of validation, 20% DNA methylation difference between the cell lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Reported as a result from pyrosequencing validation

claim: Four genes (MYH1, PCDHB16, PCDHB15, and BCL2L10) showed a differential methylation profile between metastatic and primary tumour tissue samples.
source: Next, we assessed the methylation profile of the eight selected genes in 20 tumour tissues from melanoma patients of which 10 were from metastatic melanomas and 10 were from primary melanomas (Figure 1C). Four genes (MYH1, PCDHB16, PCDHB15, and BCL2L10) showed a differential methylation profile between metastatic and primary tumour tissue samples (data not shown).
evidence: Reported as a result from patient sample analysis

claim: DNA methylation at the four selected genes could be reversed in WM266-4 cells using a low dose of 5AzadC treatment (32, 100, and 320 nM).
source: DNA methylation levels at each CpG site were analysed by bisulfite pyrosequencing, confirming a clear difference in methylation for the four genes in the aggressive tumour cells compared to less aggressive forms. Interestingly, this DNA methylation could be reversed in WM266-4 cells using a low dose of 5AzadC treatment (32, 100, and 320 nM).
evidence: Reported as a result from 5AzadC treatment experiment shown in Figure 3

claim: The median of DNA methylation within primary samples appeared to be inversely correlated with patient OS.
source: The median methylation of these individual CpGs was determined on the first set of patient samples, 10 metastatic and 10 primary tumours, and on additional 10 primary tumour samples (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). Remarkably, the median of DNA methylation within primary samples appeared to be inversely correlated with patient OS.
evidence: Reported as an observation from patient sample analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The DNA methylation profile in primary tumours with short survival is similar to that observed in metastatic patients.
source: The DNA methylation profile in primary tumours with SS similar to that observed in metastatic patients (top, in red, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Reported as an observation from patient sample analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: MYH1 was globally hypomethylated in short survival patients.
source: The analysis showed that MYH1 was globally hypomethylated in SS patients, whereas PCDHB16, PCDHB15, and BCL2L10 were hypermethylated.
evidence: Reported as a result from patient sample analysis

claim: PCDHB16, PCDHB15, and BCL2L10 were hypermethylated in short survival patients.
source: The analysis showed that MYH1 was globally hypomethylated in SS patients, whereas PCDHB16, PCDHB15, and BCL2L10 were hypermethylated.
evidence: Reported as a result from patient sample analysis

claim: The extended cohort of patients with primary melanoma (n = 49) confirmed that the four differentially methylated genes represent specific markers of more aggressive short survival primary and metastatic melanoma tumours.
source: Data from 29 additional primary tumours samples were then analysed. The extended cohort of patient with primary melanoma primary (n = 49) confirmed that these four differentially methylated genes represent specific markers of more aggressive SS primary and metastatic melanoma tumours (Figure 4A).
evidence: Reported as a result from extended patient cohort analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: One CpG showed significantly differential methylation in primary samples from short survival patients compared to long survival patients for PCDHB15, PCDBH16, and MYH1.
source: One CpG showed significantly differential methylated in primary samples from SS patients (median SS = 6 months) when compared to LS patients (median LS = 51 months) for PCDHB15, PCDBH16, and MYH1, and two CpGs for BCL2L10 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Reported as a result from CpG-level analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: Two CpGs showed significantly differential methylation in primary samples from short survival patients compared to long survival patients for BCL2L10.
source: One CpG showed significantly differential methylated in primary samples from SS patients (median SS = 6 months) when compared to LS patients (median LS = 51 months) for PCDHB15, PCDBH16, and MYH1, and two CpGs for BCL2L10 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Reported as a result from CpG-level analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: DNA methylation of MYH1 CpG was inversely correlated with survival duration and was significantly hypomethylated in primary samples from short survival patients.
source: DNA methylation MYH1 CpG was inversely correlated with survival duration and was significantly hypomethylated in primary samples from SS patients; whereas PCDHB16, PCDHB15, and BCL2L10 CpGs were hypermethylated in SS patients.
evidence: Reported as a result from correlation analysis

claim: PCDHB16, PCDHB15, and BCL2L10 CpGs were hypermethylated in short survival patients.
source: DNA methylation MYH1 CpG was inversely correlated with survival duration and was significantly hypomethylated in primary samples from SS patients; whereas PCDHB16, PCDHB15, and BCL2L10 CpGs were hypermethylated in SS patients.
evidence: Reported as a result from correlation analysis

claim: Patients with a methylation score ≥2 had a shorter life expectancy (≤1 year) than those with a methylation score value <2.
source: Patients with a methylation score ≥2 (red line) had a shorter life expectancy (≤1 year) than those with a methylation score value <2 (blue line).
evidence: Reported as a result from survival analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: A methylation score of at least 2 in primary melanoma samples is predictive of patient outcome (log-rank test, p=0.0008).
source: This analysis demonstrated that a methylation score of at least 2 in primary melanoma samples is predictive of patient outcome (log-rank test, p=0.0008) with a significant hazard ratio of 3.4 (p=0.001, concordance index = 0.62; Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Reported as a result from statistical survival analysis

claim: The methylation score has a significant hazard ratio of 3.4 (p=0.001, concordance index = 0.62).
source: This analysis demonstrated that a methylation score of at least 2 in primary melanoma samples is predictive of patient outcome (log-rank test, p=0.0008) with a significant hazard ratio of 3.4 (p=0.001, concordance index = 0.62; Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Reported as a result from hazard ratio analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B

claim: An increased Breslow depth of the primary tumour is a prognostic factor for survival probability.
source: Based on the melanoma American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging (T1, T2, T3, and T4), we confirmed that on our 49 patient samples, an increased Breslow depth of the primary tumour is a prognostic factor for survival probability (Kaplan–Meier plot in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Reported as a result from survival analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C

claim: No statistical difference was obtained between the two Breslow index groups (below 2 mm vs above 2 mm) in the study cohort.
source: We obtained no statistical difference between the two groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and E) in contrast to what obtain upon use of the methylation signature (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Reported as a result from survival analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and E

claim: The interaction between the methylation score and the Breslow index gave a significant increase of the hazard ratio from 3.4 to 6.3 (p<0.001, concordance index = 0.63).
source: Most interestingly, the interaction between the methylation score and the Breslow index gave a significant increase of the hazard ratio from 3.4 to 6.3 (p<0,001, concordance index = 0.63, Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Reported as a result from interaction analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2F

claim: The methylation score could improve the clinical prognostic utility of the Breslow index.
source: This result support that the methylation score could improve the clinical prognostic utility of the Breslow index.
evidence: Inferred from the increased hazard ratio when combining methylation score with Breslow index

claim: Common DNA methylation changes acquired by the most aggressive cells in different in vivo contexts (human, mouse, and rat) would highlight a robust and relevant trait of melanoma tumour cell plasticity and aggressiveness despite their heterogeneity.
source: We reasoned that since epigenetic changes are linked to cell plasticity and biological environment changes (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Feinberg and Fallin, 2015; Feinberg et al., 2006), any common DNA methylation changes acquired by the most aggressive cells in different in vivo contexts (human, mouse, and rat) would highlight a robust and relevant trait of melanoma tumour cell plasticity and aggressiveness despite their heterogeneity.
evidence: Based on reasoning from cited literature about epigenetic changes and cell plasticity

claim: Epigenetic changes are linked to cell plasticity and biological environment changes.
source: We reasoned that since epigenetic changes are linked to cell plasticity and biological environment changes (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Feinberg and Fallin, 2015; Feinberg et al., 2006), any common DNA methylation changes acquired by the most aggressive cells in different in vivo contexts (human, mouse, and rat) would highlight a robust and relevant trait of melanoma tumour cell plasticity and aggressiveness despite their heterogeneity.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Feinberg and Fallin, 2015; Feinberg et al., 2006

claim: Melanoma is a highly heterogeneous tumour.
source: Indeed, melanoma is highly heterogeneous tumour, and until now it has been difficult to find a signature in primary melanoma, either based on DNA methylation or gene expression that help to predict prognosis as well as Breslow index (Bhalla et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation to Bhalla et al., 2019

claim: Until now it has been difficult to find a signature in primary melanoma, either based on DNA methylation or gene expression that help to predict prognosis as well as Breslow index.
source: Indeed, melanoma is highly heterogeneous tumour, and until now it has been difficult to find a signature in primary melanoma, either based on DNA methylation or gene expression that help to predict prognosis as well as Breslow index (Bhalla et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bhalla et al., 2019

claim: The observation of clustered genes regulated by DNA methylation is reminiscent of the mechanism underlying parental imprinting and its spreading on imprinted genes during development.
source: This observation of clustered genes regulated by DNA methylation is reminiscent of the mechanism underlying parental imprinting and its spreading on imprinted genes during development (Lewis and Reik, 2006; Lindsay and Adams, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lewis and Reik, 2006 and Lindsay and Adams, 1996

claim: The clustering observation is coherent with the association of hypermethylated regions with long range epigenetic silencing (LRES) described in colon cancer.
source: It is also coherent with the association of hypermethylated regions with long range epigenetic silencing (LRES) described by Frigola et al., 2006 in colon cancer and with the fact that LRES regions containing hypermethylated genes extend up to 4 Mb and are correlated with gene extinction (Coolen et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Frigola et al., 2006 and Coolen et al., 2010

claim: LRES regions containing hypermethylated genes extend up to 4 Mb and are correlated with gene extinction.
source: It is also coherent with the association of hypermethylated regions with long range epigenetic silencing (LRES) described by Frigola et al., 2006 in colon cancer and with the fact that LRES regions containing hypermethylated genes extend up to 4 Mb and are correlated with gene extinction (Coolen et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coolen et al., 2010

claim: All four validated genes are demethylated upon treatment with 5AzadC in WM266-4 metastatic melanoma cells.
source: All four genes are demethylated upon treatment with 5AzadC in WM266-4 metastatic melanoma cells and displayed the strongest methylation differential.
evidence: Reported as a result from 5AzadC treatment experiment

claim: Five CpGs were significantly differentially methylated between patients with a short OS (<1 year) and those with a longer OS (>1 year).
source: In the last part of our study, we challenged the methylation status of these four gene promoters in 59 patient samples. Surprisingly, five CpGs were significantly differentially methylated between patients with a short OS (<1 year, SS) and those with a longer OS (>1 year, LS).
evidence: Reported as a result from patient sample analysis

claim: The study discovered an early and robust signature of melanoma progression based directly on the primary tumour that can significantly predict patient outcome (p=0.0008).
source: This led to the discovery of an early and robust signature of melanoma progression that is only based directly on the primary tumour that can significantly predict patient outcome (p=0.0008).
evidence: Reported as a main finding from the study

claim: Only one study has reported a difference in methylation profile among primary tumour samples linking it to an ulceration status and thus a poor clinical outcome.
